$schema_note: IPP transport-binding conformance fixture. Normative companion to 06-ipp/6.6-transport-bindings.md. Object keys are wire form (snake_case), per 06-ipp/6.1 JSON format. Run 06-ipp/conformance/validate.mjs to check this file's own self-consistency.

link_url_grammar.wire_rule_criterion: Every rule here is decidable from this text alone. A rule of the form 'equals what my parser produces' is NOT a wire rule: two parsers normalize differently, so the text agrees while the judges disagree. That mistake was made once on this protocol -- 'the parsed path must equal the raw path' -- and produced a measured three-character divergence (| and ^ and a malformed percent escape). It is replaced by the explicit character sets below.
link_url_grammar.applies_to: Every check below is applied to the RAW input URL string: not percent-decoded, not dot-segment-folded, not otherwise normalized, and NOT re-serialized by a URL parser first. A URL is shape-valid iff it matches url_regex, does NOT match forbidden_path_segment_regex, and passes the authority and port rules below.
link_url_grammar.applies_to_rationale: Go's url.Parse().Path percent-decodes (%61 becomes 'a', so a token carrying a percent escape would pass a naive check) -- use EscapedPath() or the raw string. WHATWG URL (browsers) folds dot segments and strips leading/trailing whitespace before pathname is readable. Both make a parsed URL the wrong thing to test.

path_segment_rules.charset: Each path segment MUST consist only of RFC 3986 pchar: unreserved (A-Za-z0-9-._~), pct-encoded, sub-delims (!$&'()*+,;=), ':' and '@'.
path_segment_rules.pct_encoded: A '%' MUST be followed by exactly two hex digits, and those digits MUST BE UPPERCASE ('%2F' is legal, '%2f' is rejected). A malformed escape is rejected outright, never repaired.
path_segment_rules.pct_hex_case_rationale: Rule 9 is strict string equality, while RFC 3986 section 6.2.2.1 says pct-encoded hex digits SHOULD be normalized to uppercase before comparing -- so 'normalize it' is a defensible reading and the two readings disagree. Measured on one code: a link URL deriving 'https://gw.example.com/a%41%2Fb' against payload.endpoint 'https://gw.example.com/a%41%2fb' is UNEQUAL under strict equality (refuse) and EQUAL after section 6.2.2.1 normalization (pay). Ruled REJECT rather than normalize, in line with scheme / port / IPv6: this list rejects non-canonical spellings everywhere rather than folding them. The cost is near zero because Go's url.QueryEscape and JavaScript's encodeURIComponent both emit uppercase, so real issuers are unaffected; only hand-written URLs are, and those should follow the spec anyway.
path_segment_rules.no_dot_segment: No '.' or '..' segment, in any spelling including '%2e' / '%2E'. Rejected outright, never folded.
path_segment_rules.why_charset_not_normal_form: '|' and '^' are the concrete reason. They are not pchar, but a parser-based rule disagreed about them: Go re-serializes them as %7C / %5E (so a 'raw == normalized' test rejects) while WHATWG leaves them (so the same test accepts). The character set decides both cases identically without consulting either parser.

scheme_rule.rule: The scheme MUST be the lowercase literal 'https'. 'HTTPS://' and any other casing MUST be rejected -- rejected, NOT lowercased.
scheme_rule.rationale: RFC 3986 section 3.1 makes schemes case-insensitive, so 'normalize it' is a defensible reading, and an earlier version of the normalization steps said 'lowercase the scheme', which implied a mixed-case scheme would arrive and be folded. Two readings, opposite answers for 'HTTPS://pay.example.com/ipp/v1/link/<t>'. Every other component here rejects the non-canonical spelling rather than normalizing it (port, path, IPv6); the scheme being the sole exception is what made it ambiguous. Note the contrast with the HOST, which IS accepted and lowercased -- DNS is genuinely case-insensitive and payload.endpoint may legitimately arrive uppercase. The two directions differ, so both need a case.

authority_rules.ascii_only: The authority MUST be entirely ASCII. Any code point >= U+0080 is rejected. The interoperable spelling for an internationalized host is punycode.
authority_rules.ascii_only_rationale: Closes three measured divergences at once: C1 control characters inside the authority; IDN (one side keeps raw UTF-8 and lowercases per Unicode, the other applies UTS-46 + punycode, so the two derived endpoints can never be equal); and U+200B ZERO WIDTH SPACE, which UTS-46 mapping DELETES -- one side then derives 'pay.example.com' from 'pay\u200b.example.com' and sends a request to a host that is not the one in the URL.

forms.note: Exactly one of the three, then an optional port. Which form applies is decided by the text, not by a parser: bracketed means IPv6, else a dotted quad matching ipv4_regex means IPv4, else reg-name.

reg_name.rule: Dot-separated LDH labels per RFC 1123: letters, digits and hyphens; each label 1-63 characters; a label MUST NOT begin or end with a hyphen; no empty label, so no trailing dot ('pay.example.com.' and 'h.' are rejected).
reg_name.stricter_than_whatwg: The trailing dot, the length bound and the hyphen positions are all stricter than WHATWG URL, which checks none of the three. Deliberate: they are part of the RFC 1123 definition of an LDH label, so anyone implementing 'LDH label' from the text alone will already do them, and leaving them unsaid is the ambiguity the wire-rule criterion warns about. None of the three resolves in practice, so the tightening costs nothing.
reg_name.rightmost_label_rule: The rightmost label MUST NOT 'end in a number' in the WHATWG URL sense: it MUST NOT be all ASCII digits, and MUST NOT start with '0x' or '0X'. '0x7f000001' is a perfectly legal LDH label, so an implementation following 'LDH labels only' to the letter accepts it while WHATWG rewrites it to 127.0.0.1 -- the same divergence again. The one judgement covers '3405803625', '203.0.113' and '0x7f000001' together. No real TLD is all digits or 0x-prefixed, so the tightening costs nothing.

ipv4.rule: Dotted decimal, exactly four octets, each 0-255, NO leading zeros.
ipv4.rationale: '01.2.3.4', '1.2.3.04' and '0177.0.0.1' are rejected. Left open, one side reads a leading zero as decimal and another as octal -- 0177.0.0.1 is 127.0.0.1 to the second.

ipv6.rule: Bracketed, lowercase hex, and in RFC 5952 canonical form.
rfc5952_subrules: 4.2.1 -- a SINGLE zero group is NOT compressed ('2001:db8:0:1:1:1:1:1', never '2001:db8::1:1:1:1:1')
4.2.2 -- '::' only compresses a run of TWO OR MORE zero groups
4.2.3 -- when two zero runs tie for longest, compress the LEFTMOST ('1::1:0:0:1:1' and '1:0:0:1::1:1' are the same address written two ways; without this rule the two sides pick different runs)
4.1 -- no leading zeros inside a group ('::01' is not canonical, '::1' is)

dotted_tail.note: A dotted IPv4 tail is REQUIRED for exactly one form and rejected everywhere else. Read all four rows; the middle two are the ones that get implemented backwards.

table.why: this IS the canonical form of an IPv4-mapped address (RFC 5952 section 5)
pure hex is NOT the canonical form of an IPv4-mapped address. Note a WHATWG serializer emits exactly this spelling; RFC 5952 governs here
IPv4-COMPATIBLE (::/96), deprecated by RFC 4291. The mixed notation is not offered for it
mixed notation is only for IPv4-mapped

ipv6.rejection_not_serialization: This is a REJECTION rule, not a production rule: an implementation only has to judge the string as written. It does NOT need its own RFC 5952 serializer, and MUST NOT rewrite a non-canonical host into a canonical one and proceed.
ipv6.rationale: Measured: link URL '[2001:db8:0:0:0:0:0:1]' with payload.endpoint '[2001:db8::1]' -- one implementation canonicalizes the host and pays, the other lowercases only and refuses. Other measured shapes: '[0::1]', '[::01]', '[::ffff:127.0.0.1]'. RFC 5952 is a written algorithm, so every implementation can judge without consulting a library.

port.rule: Canonical spelling only: no leading zeros, no empty port (':' with nothing after it), and the value MUST be in 1-65535. Port 0 is rejected too -- it breaks none of the other three prohibitions, so reading them literally would let it through.
port.rationale: ':0443' derives 'https://h:0443' where a port is compared as a string and 'https://h' where it is parsed as a number -- one side pays, the other refuses. ':99999' is kept by one parser and thrown out by another. Rejecting the non-canonical spelling is cheaper than making every implementation agree on how to normalize it.

forbidden_code_points.note: Rejected anywhere in the string. Given as code points on purpose -- see forbidden_char_note. For URL shape these are already excluded by the character sets above; the rule earns its keep on payload.endpoint, and because a parser may STRIP some of them and hand back a string that then looks valid.

classes.name: whitespace
classes.detail: space and the ASCII whitespace characters

classes.name: C1
classes.why: Go's unicode.IsSpace matches U+0085 (NEL); JavaScript's \s does not. Naming the range makes both sides agree.

classes.name: BOM
classes.why: The mirror image: JavaScript's \s matches U+FEFF, Go's unicode.IsSpace does not. With C1 and BOM both named, the two whitespace sets are finally equal.

forbidden_code_points.forbidden_char_note: Deliberately NOT given as a regex literal to copy. Two wrong shapes have both really occurred: (a) a stray character inside a whitespace class -- '[\s -]' also matches a literal '-', which rejects any host like 'api-test.example.fi' and any token containing '-'; it is NOT a range and does not touch '+' or ','; (b) a genuine range with punctuation endpoints -- '[ -,]' is U+0020..U+002C and swallows '+' and ','. Self-check for BOTH shapes: '\s' appearing inside a character class, and a '-' whose neighbours are not alphanumeric. Checking only for 'a range' misses (a), which is the one that actually shipped. Neither surfaces on the happy path: an all-letter token and a hyphen-free host pass straight through to production.

link_url_grammar.endpoint_derivation: Strip the trailing '/ipp/v1/link/{link_token}' from the raw URL; whatever remains (scheme://authority plus any path prefix) is the endpoint.

ordered_steps: 1. lowercase the authority (the scheme is NOT normalized -- only lowercase 'https' is accepted in the first place, see authority_rules.scheme)
2. drop the port if it equals the scheme default (443 for https)
4. only then check that the remaining path is empty or a sequence of non-empty segments
normalization.pct_encoding_does_not_participate: Percent-encoding is NOT normalized here -- not decoded, and not case-folded. It does not need to be: a non-canonical spelling (lowercase hex, or a malformed escape) has already been rejected at the shape layer, so by the time two endpoints are compared both carry uppercase hex. Stated explicitly because its absence from the step list reads like an omission.
normalization.order_is_normative: Step 4 MUST come after step 3. Reversed, 'https://h/api/' is judged to have an empty last segment and a perfectly legal payload.endpoint is refused.
normalization.note: The derived endpoint never carries a trailing slash (the prefix is whatever precedes '/ipp/v1/link/'). payload.endpoint may, so 'https://h', 'https://h/' and 'https://h//' all normalize to 'https://h'.

payload_endpoint_checks.applies: payload.endpoint receives EVERY check the link URL receives -- forbidden code points, ASCII-only authority, authority and port canonical form, no userinfo, no query, no fragment, no backslash, no empty segment, and NO dot segment.
payload_endpoint_checks.does_not_apply: Only the '/ipp/v1/link/{link_token}' suffix shape, because payload.endpoint is not the scanned URL.
payload_endpoint_checks.rationale: An earlier version excused payload.endpoint from the dot-segment and backslash rules on the grounds that it is not the scanned string. Measured result: 'https://h/api/../api' stays as written where the escaped path is read and folds to 'https://h/api' where WHATWG's pathname is read -- against link URL 'https://h/api/ipp/v1/link/<t>' one implementation pays and the other refuses. 'https://good.com\evil.com' likewise errors on one side and folds to 'https://good.com/evil.com' on the other. The root cause is the same both times: saying 'this rule does not apply' never defined what the canonical spelling IS, and the two parsers answered differently. Applying one identical set of checks is the only answer both sides can reach, and no legitimate payload carries a dot segment or a backslash, so the tightening costs nothing.

envelope.consumer_rule: A response carrying any top-level key outside this set MUST be rejected. `type` MUST be 'request'.
envelope.body_encoding: The body MUST be a bare JSON IPPMessage. The compact 'ipp1:' string MUST NOT be accepted here even by an implementation whose shared decoder understands it, and encoding MUST NOT be sniffed: the request already declared `Accept: application/json`, so a second accepted encoding buys nothing and gives two implementations something to disagree about.
envelope.body_encoding_judged_on_bytes: THE JUDGEMENT IS ON BYTES, NOT CODE POINTS. Skip leading bytes 0x20, 0x09, 0x0A, 0x0D -- and only those four -- then the next byte MUST be 0x7B ('{'). The check MUST run on the raw response bytes and MUST NOT be performed after a text decoder that strips a BOM.
envelope.body_encoding_why_bytes: Third occurrence of one cause; the first two were the URL character set and 'trim'. A code-point rule is still a pseudo-wire rule here, because stripping the BOM happens at the bytes-to-text step and decoders disagree. Measured on the same input EF BB BF 7B ...: Buffer.toString('utf8') keeps U+FEFF, new TextDecoder('utf-8').decode() strips it, await new Response(b).text() strips it, Go string(b) keeps it. Two wallets that both faithfully implement the code-point rule therefore diverge: the browser / fetch().text() route never sees the BOM and PAYS, the Go route REFUSES. Measured again at the implementation layer: for a body beginning U+0085 one side accepted and the other refused; for U+FEFF the verdicts swapped. Neither side implemented the four-character set, so bodies prefixed with U+000B, U+000C, U+00A0, U+2028 or U+3000 were accepted by both -- on bytes, every one of those is rejected because its first byte is not 0x7B.
envelope.leading_bom_is_rejected: A BOM is NOT whitespace here. A body whose first three bytes are EF BB BF MUST be rejected, consistent with RFC 8259 section 8.1 ('implementations MUST NOT add a byte order mark'). Middleboxes and serializers do prepend one, so this is not hypothetical. Note the generic byte rule above already rejects it (EF is not 0x7B); this row is called out separately because it is the case an implementation is most likely to have decoded away before checking.
envelope.top_level_key_spelling: A top-level key's LITERAL SPELLING in the response bytes MUST be exactly one of the five tokens "v" "network" "type" "meta" "payload", and MUST NOT contain any backslash escape. Judged on the bytes of the key token, before any string unescaping.
envelope.top_level_key_spelling_why: Fifth occurrence of one cause, and it was introduced by the round that fixed the third one -- the duplicate-key rule below was justified as 'decidable on the bytes' while the object it constrains, a key NAME, arrives as a JSON string, and JSON strings carry backslash escapes. That transformation changes the thing being judged. Measured on {"\u0076":1,"network":...,"payload":{}} (\u0076 is 'v'): parse first and the key set is {v,network,type,payload}, a subset of the five, so ACCEPT and pay; compare raw spellings and the key is \u0076, not in the five, so REJECT. Two implementations, both following the earlier text, opposite verdicts. Banning escapes outright removes the unescaping step entirely, which puts BOTH this rule and the duplicate rule back on the bytes; it also matches how the rest of this document rejects non-canonical spellings instead of folding them. No real server has any reason to spell 'v' as '\u0076'.
envelope.no_duplicate_top_level_keys: Top-level keys MUST NOT repeat; a duplicate MUST be rejected. The 'subset of five keys' comparison happens AFTER a parser folds duplicates, and the folding semantics belong to the parser (last-one-wins, or an error). So {"v":1,...,"v":2} still presents five keys to a lenient parser and is accepted, while a strict parser errors and rejects. Measured: parsing that body yields only FOUR top-level keys, so the duplicate is invisible after parsing. Because escapes are banned above, this comparison runs on the raw key tokens with no unescaping step -- that is what makes it genuinely decidable on the bytes.
envelope.size_limit_unit: Response size limits are counted in BYTES -- both the Content-Length check and the cap applied while reading. NOT characters and NOT UTF-16 code units: a `meta` value containing non-ASCII text otherwise puts the two implementations at different effective limits for the same response. This fixture pins the UNIT, not a number; the number is an implementation choice.
envelope.forward_compatibility_commitment: A protocol commitment, not merely a validation rule. Because deployed third-party wallets reject unknown top-level keys, growing a sixth one would make all of them stop paying at once, on an upgrade schedule no single party controls. Therefore the top-level key set is CLOSED, the extension point is `meta`, and adding a top-level key is a breaking change requiring a bump of `v`. This is deliberately the opposite stance from machine codes (see 6.2), which are an OPEN string clients must tolerate not recognizing -- a code is diagnostic output, an envelope is a parsing contract.
envelope.error_envelope_shapes: TWO shapes MUST be accepted for a 4xx/5xx error body, and neither may be dropped. 6.2 documents the FLAT one -- {code, message?, param?} -- and that is what a third party implementing an IPP endpoint from the prose emits. The invisi gateway emits a Stripe-style NESTED one -- {"error":{type,code,message,param,request_id,details}} (SPEC-057, every /ipp/v1/* route). An implementation accepting only one of them throws away the machine code of every answer in the other shape, and 6.6 requires an unknown code to be PROPAGATED to the caller -- so the payer wallet loses the one field that says WHY a receiver refused. MEASURED: both SDKs accepted only the nested shape and reported every flat answer as a transport failure with no code at all.
envelope.error_envelope_shape_boundary: Only the SHAPE is negotiated. `code` stays an open string (6.2): an unrecognised value MUST be surfaced verbatim, never mapped or rejected. And recognition is not 'any JSON object': a FLAT body is one carrying a non-empty `code`, because 6.2 makes `code` the required field. That is what keeps the retired {"error":"some_string","message":"..."} shape out -- it has no `code`, so there is no machine code to surface and typing it would hand the caller an empty one. A body carrying none of the fields ({} or an unrelated object) is not the contract in either shape and MUST NOT be turned into an empty typed error.
envelope.error_envelope_shape_pairs_note: One machine code, delivered in both accepted shapes. Implementations MUST assert that the two members of a pair surface THE SAME code -- asserting each case against its own literal leaves 'both happen to be spelled link_not_found' as a coincidence in the file rather than a property a runner checks. The third pair carries an unrecognised code on purpose: widening the accepted SHAPES must not widen anything about the code, which stays an open string surfaced verbatim.

host_policy.note: Rule 4. Judge the RESOLVED address, not the literal host. Strip brackets and any zone id ('%...') before classifying. Every address a name resolves to MUST be public -- not merely the first: a name answering one public and one internal address would otherwise be a coin flip decided by whichever record the connect path picks.

blocked_ipv4.why: IETF protocol assignments. STRICTLY /24 -- the third octet is significant. Written as /16 it also swallows 192.0.2.0/24 (TEST-NET-1), which must stay public; see public_addresses

embedded_ipv4.note: An IPv4 address wearing an IPv6 costume. Unwrap the inner IPv4 and judge THAT against blocked_ipv4 -- never the wrapper. This applies to AAAA records too: a hostile NAT64 answer is a realistic way to hand a wallet an internal target that looks like a public IPv6 address.

prefixes.why: deprecated IPv4-compatible; '::7f00:1' is 127.0.0.1 and reads as public unless unwrapped

public_addresses.why: TEST-NET-1 (RFC 5737). Adjacent to 192.0.0.0/24 and the exact value an over-broad /16 would wrongly block
just above 100.64.0.0/10; guards against CGNAT written as 100/8
just above 172.16.0.0/12; guards against RFC 1918 written as 172/8
an ordinary public IPv6 in canonical form
just below the fc00::/7 and fe80::/10 boundaries; guards against ULA written as f000::/4

failure_modes.fail_closed: Where the host runtime IS capable of name resolution, failing to obtain that capability MUST throw. It MUST NOT silently fall back to the degraded name heuristic -- that fallback is reserved for runtimes with no name resolution at all (browsers). Otherwise a stubbed module specifier, a permission-restricted import or a repackaged bundle silently downgrades the strictest runtime to the weakest check with nothing surfaced to the caller.
failure_modes.resolution_failure_is_transport: A name that cannot be resolved (offline, DNS down, NXDOMAIN, zero addresses) MUST raise a TRANSPORT-class error, never the rule-4 security error. Reporting it as a security verdict makes the wallet tell the user 'refused to resolve this host', which reads as 'this code is dangerous' rather than 'you have no network'.
failure_modes.indeterminate_status: Applies ONLY to runtimes whose transport can hand back a response with no readable HTTP status (a browser fetch returning an opaque response). Runtimes with no such channel -- a Go or Rust HTTP client always yields either a status or an error -- have nothing to implement here. Where it does apply: such a response MUST NOT be reported as a refused redirect unless the runtime positively identifies it as an opaque redirect; otherwise report a transport error. MUST NOT fabricate a 3xx status code that was never observed.
failure_modes.client_rejection_carries_no_machine_code: The machine codes in 6.2 are a SERVER contract. A rejection decided locally by the client -- every rule in this document -- carries no machine code and no stable classification. A caller MUST NOT branch on anything beyond 'this was rejected': not on message text, not on error subtype, not on whether the reason was a shape violation versus an endpoint mismatch. Implementations legitimately differ here (one may wrap two sentinels, another may throw a single error with a cause) and nothing on the wire distinguishes them, so any caller branching on it is depending on one implementation's internals.

applies_to: the cap applied while reading the body
response_limits.note: Counted in BYTES, not characters and not UTF-16 code units. A `meta` value carrying non-ASCII text otherwise leaves two implementations at different effective limits for the same response. The NUMBER is an implementation choice; the unit is not.

resolve_request.note: No credentials, no cookies, no fingerprintable custom headers. Redirects MUST NOT be followed (rule 6).

codec_pairs.note: Decoding `compact` MUST yield `messages[message_ref]`. Re-encoding MAY produce a different byte order (MessagePack map ordering is implementation-defined); assert on the decoded value, never on the string.
Same envelope reachable through both carriers; `endpoint` here carries an explicit default port.

accept.note: reg-name is compared case-insensitively; the token is NOT case-folded.
Non-default port kept, and kept on both sides of the cross-check.
A hyphen in an LDH label is legal. This is the exact host shape the '[\s -]' bug rejected, and the token below also carries a hyphen-free spelling — keep both.
22 chars including a '-'. Rejected by the '[\s -]' bug while an all-letter sample passed.
Path prefixes are legal: IPP mounted behind a shared gateway. Only the SUFFIX is fixed; the prefix rides into the derived endpoint.
Every RFC 3986 sub-delim plus ':' and '@' in one segment. All pchar, so all legal — an implementation that hand-rolled a narrower set fails here.
Well-formed pct-encoded stays RAW in the derived endpoint. Decoding it would turn %2F into a path separator and change the endpoint.
RFC 5952 canonical: lowercase, maximal zero compression. The non-canonical spelling of the same address is rejected below.
The canonical form of an IPv4-mapped address per RFC 5952 section 5 — the ONE place a dotted tail is required rather than rejected. 1.2.3.4 is public, so the host policy lets it through too.
63 characters is the RFC 1123 maximum and MUST be accepted; 64 is rejected.

RFC 5952 4.2.3 POSITIVE control: two zero runs tie for longest, the LEFTMOST is compressed, and this spelling is therefore canonical and MUST be accepted. Its mirror reject case is reject-authority-ipv6-tie-not-leftmost-2, the same address with the rightmost run compressed. Without this accept case an implementation that simply rejects any address containing two equal zero runs passes every reject case in this file.

RFC 5952 4.2.1 POSITIVE control: a SINGLE zero group is written out, not compressed, so this spelling is canonical and MUST be accepted. Its mirror reject case is reject-authority-ipv6-single-zero-group-compressed. Without this accept case an implementation that rejects any address containing a literal '0' group passes every reject case in this file.
65535 is exactly the upper bound and MUST be accepted. Without this, '< 65535' and '<= 65536' both pass every reject case (the only reject is :99999).

reject.reason: scheme is not https

uppercase scheme. RFC 3986 section 3.1 makes schemes case-insensitive, so 'lowercase it and continue' is a defensible reading — this rule picks REJECT instead, matching how port / path / IPv6 all reject non-canonical spellings rather than normalizing them. Contrast accept-uppercase-host, where the HOST is accepted and lowercased
compact carrier, not a link URL
userinfo; the real host is evil.example.net while a human reads good.example.com
userinfo
query component present
fragment component present
path does not end with the /ipp/v1/link/{token} suffix — the /ipp/v1 namespace is missing. Path PREFIXES are legal (see accept-path-prefix); what is fixed is the suffix
the token must be the LAST segment
trailing slash is an extra empty segment after the token
empty path segment ('//'); parsers disagree on whether to collapse it, so the derived endpoint would differ
'..' path segment. Rejected outright, never folded: one parser leaves it and WHATWG folds it, so the two derive different endpoints from the same QR code
'.' path segment; same fold-divergence as '..'

'%2E%2E' is a '..' segment in another spelling. Written UPPERCASE on purpose so it is charset-legal and therefore ISOLATES the dot-segment rule — the lowercase spelling would also trip the hex-case rule and the case would no longer pin what it claims to

lowercase pct-encoded hex. MEASURED as a pay/refuse divergence: rule 9 is strict equality, but RFC 3986 section 6.2.2.1 says normalize pct hex to uppercase before comparing — so link URL '/a%41%2Fb' against payload.endpoint '/a%41%2fb' is unequal (refuse) under one reading and equal (pay) under the other. Ruled reject, matching scheme / port / IPv6
one escape uppercase, one lowercase — a partial implementation that only uppercases the first escape still fails here
'|' is not pchar. MEASURED DIVERGENCE under the old 'raw equals normalized' rule: one parser re-serializes it as %7C and rejected, WHATWG left it and accepted
'^' is not pchar; same measured divergence as '|'
'%' not followed by two hex digits. MEASURED DIVERGENCE: one parser errors ('invalid URL escape'), WHATWG accepts it verbatim. Rejected outright, never repaired
'%2' at the end of the token segment: truncated escape AND not base64url
21 characters
23 characters
'+' is standard base64, not base64url
percent-encoding in the token segment. Only rejected if the check runs on the RAW string — a parser that decodes %61 to 'a' would accept it
WHATWG reads a backslash in the authority as a path separator (host good.example.com), another parser does not (host is the whole string). One written link, two origins
empty rightmost label. One side treats the root-label dot as significant, another strips it
an LDH label must not begin with a hyphen
'%' is not legal in a reg-name. MEASURED: one side maps it to host 'h.', another rejects outright
64-character label; RFC 1123 caps an LDH label at 63
rightmost label starts with '0x' — WHATWG 'ends in a number' treats the host as an IPv4 literal
'_' is not an LDH character
all-digit host. MEASURED: read as the IPv4 literal 203.0.113.105 by one implementation and as a DNS name by another
0x-prefixed host. MEASURED: read as 127.0.0.1 by one implementation and as a DNS name by another — this one reaches loopback
three-part dotted number. MEASURED: completed to 203.0.0.113 by one implementation, treated as a DNS name by another
leading zero in the first octet; also an all-digit rightmost label
leading zero in the last octet
octal spelling of 127.0.0.1. MEASURED: reaches loopback on any implementation that parses a leading zero as octal
octet > 255
not RFC 5952 canonical (zero run not compressed). MEASURED: against payload.endpoint '[2001:db8::1]' one implementation canonicalizes and pays, another lowercases only and refuses
leading zero in a group; canonical is '::1'
uppercase hex; RFC 5952 requires lowercase

an IPv4-mapped address written in pure hex. RFC 5952 section 5 makes '[::ffff:127.0.0.1]' the canonical form, so this spelling is rejected. A WHATWG serializer emits exactly this — RFC 5952 governs here

IPv4-COMPATIBLE (::/96), deprecated by RFC 4291; the mixed notation is not offered for it. Its canonical hex spelling '[::7f00:1]' is a legal shape and is caught one step later by the host policy instead
mixed notation outside ::ffff:0:0/96
measured trigger shape; canonical is '[::1]'
RFC 5952 4.2.3: two zero runs tie, so the LEFTMOST is compressed — canonical is '[1::1:0:0:1:1]'. Same address, two spellings; without the tie-break the two sides pick different runs

reject_contract.isolates: A case carrying `isolates: true` MUST trip exactly ONE named check. Its whole purpose is to pin that one rule, so an edit that makes another check fire too silently destroys it -- the case still goes red, so nothing looks wrong, while the rule it was written for is no longer the reason. Measured: rewriting reject-path-percent-encoded-dot-segment with lowercase hex makes the charset rule fire alongside the dot-segment rule, and the case stops pinning either one. validate.mjs enforces the count.
reject_contract.assert_the_reason: A case that only asserts 'this was rejected' is a false green for the rule it names in `rejected_by`. Most of these URLs trip more than one check, so removing the rule under test leaves another one to catch it and the case stays green. Assert the REASON (which check fired), and verify it by short-circuiting the named rule: exactly the cases naming it must go red. Measured three times on this protocol — dot-segment, C1-control and backslash cases were all being caught by a since-removed 'path is not in normal form' check rather than by the rule they claimed to test.
reject_contract.also_rejected_by: Computed by validate.mjs, not hand-maintained. It lists every other named check that also rejects the URL, so a case that cannot isolate its rule is visible rather than assumed.
reject_contract.invisible_characters: Cases whose input contains a character an editor may silently normalize away carry `url_template` + `codepoint` INSTEAD of `url`. Build the input with String.fromCodePoint / rune conversion; never paste the character into a source file. Such characters live only in reject cases, so if a formatter eats one the suite stays green while the rule loses its only test.
reject_contract.requires_note: An entry carrying `requires` needs a runtime capability the host environment may not have. An implementation without that capability MUST skip the case explicitly and MUST document the gap — it MUST NOT report the case as passing. The exception is `local_name: true`, which the degraded form must also catch.

required_controls.note: Cases that MUST exist. Deleting any of them -- or never adding it, which is what actually happened once -- leaves a hole that NOTHING else in this file reports: a reject-only suite is passed by an over-tight implementation, and per-rule coverage is satisfied by any one case naming the rule, so a distinct FACET of a rule can vanish silently. validate.mjs asserts every id below is present.

ids.why: RFC 5952 4.2.3 positive. Without it, 'reject any address with two equal zero runs' passes everything
RFC 5952 4.2.1 positive. Without it, 'reject any address containing a literal 0 group' passes everything
the ONE dotted tail that must be accepted; without it 'reject all dotted tails' passes everything
the exact upper bound. Without it '< 65535' and '<= 65536' both pass
host IS normalized, unlike the scheme. The two directions differ and both need a case
scheme is REJECTED, not normalized. Per-rule coverage is already satisfied by the other two scheme cases, so this facet needs naming or it can vanish silently
the exact host shape the '[\s -]' bug rejected
the exact token shape that bug rejected; an all-letter sample hides it
RFC 1123 upper bound, positive side
path prefixes are legal; without it 'exact path match' passes every reject case
the full sub-delims set is legal; a hand-rolled narrower set fails only here
pct-encoding stays RAW in the derived endpoint, and UPPERCASE hex is the legal spelling — without it 'reject every pct escape' passes every reject case
the four skippable bytes; without it 'reject any leading byte' passes every body reject
the prefix participates in the cross-check
trailing slashes are stripped, not rejected
the only case an addresses[0]-only implementation fails
the FLAT envelope shape (6.2). Without it a nested-only reader passes every case and silently drops the machine code of every third-party resolver
the NESTED envelope shape (SPEC-057). The pair is the control: either shape alone is satisfied by a reader that only understands that one
the boundary of the flat reading. Without it, 'any object carrying a message' passes every other case while handing callers an empty machine code
the open-string property in the nested shape. Without it, 'unknown codes propagate' is only ever exercised through one envelope shape

resolve_contract.assert_every_expect_key: Every key present in a case's `expect` object MUST be asserted, not just `outcome`. A runner that switches on `outcome` alone reports resolve-accept-expired-envelope as passing while never testing expiry detection at all -- the flag `envelope_expired` is the entire point of that case. The same applies to `endpoint`, `message_ref`, `rule`, `error_code` and `http_status`.
resolve_contract.unknown_expect_key: An `expect` key this runner does not understand MUST fail loudly, never be skipped: a silently ignored key is a conformance claim with nothing behind it.
resolve_contract.envelope_expired_means: `envelope_expired: true` asserts that meta.expiresAt REACHES THE CALLER and is in the past -- not that the implementation exposes a dedicated expiry flag. An earlier wording demanded a separate signal, which is a requirement 6.6 places on the wallet rather than on the resolver; both SDKs pass meta through and neither has such a flag.

expect.note: Derived endpoint has no port, payload.endpoint has :443; equal after normalization (rule 9).
Rule 9 compares the FULL derived endpoint including the path prefix. An implementation that drops the prefix derives https://pay.example.com and fails this case.
payload.endpoint is 'https://pay.example.com/'; the derived endpoint never carries a trailing slash. Strip trailing slashes before comparing or this legal code is rejected.

meta.expiresAt is in the past while the server still answered 200. Resolution succeeds. What the RESOLVER owes its caller is that meta arrives intact, because meta.expiresAt IS the expiry signal -- 6.6 puts the check-before-display SHOULD on the WALLET, not on the resolver, so a dedicated flag is not required of an SDK. An implementation that drops or rewrites meta on the way through takes the signal away from the only layer that can act on it. Assert that meta.expiresAt reaches the caller and parses as a past instant.

expect.reason: derived endpoint is https://pay.example.com/api but payload.endpoint is https://pay.example.com — the path prefix is part of the endpoint and MUST participate in the cross-check
payload.endpoint is a different host than the one the link URL was fetched from

the envelope carries no endpoint, and a scan-distributed request MUST carry one (6.1). DECLARED AS RULE 8, NOT 9, on purpose: `mode` is required and is always 'single' or 'multi' (6.1), each of which makes `endpoint` required, so the shared decoder's baseline validation refuses this body before the rule-9 cross-check is reached. Rule 9's own 'no endpoint to compare against' branch is therefore not reachable through the public entry point by any LEGAL body, and no case here claims to isolate it -- claiming so was a W15 false isolation: the case stayed red while the rule it named was not the reason.

payload.endpoint is 'https://pay.example.com/api/../api'. MEASURED DIVERGENCE: left as written where the escaped path is read, folded to '/api' where WHATWG's pathname is read — the folding side would find it EQUAL to the derived endpoint and pay. payload.endpoint gets the same dot-segment rejection as the link URL, so both sides refuse
payload.endpoint contains a backslash in the authority. MEASURED: errors on one parser, folds to 'https://good.example.com/evil.example.net' on another

payload.endpoint spells the same bytes with LOWERCASE pct hex ('/a%41%2fb' vs the derived '/a%41%2Fb'). Strict equality refuses; an implementation that applies RFC 3986 section 6.2.2.1 normalization before comparing finds them equal and PAYS. payload.endpoint receives the same uppercase-hex rule as the link URL, so both sides refuse

payload.endpoint is '[2001:db8:0:0:0:0:0:1]', the same address as the link URL host but not in RFC 5952 canonical form. MEASURED: an implementation that canonicalizes the host finds them equal and pays; one that only lowercases refuses. Requiring canonical form on BOTH sides makes every implementation refuse
3xx; following it would let another host supply the JSON representation and the derived endpoint would no longer describe who answered
any 3xx is a failure, including same-host; 'same host' is not an exemption a third party can be trusted to evaluate identically
type is voucher, not request; IPPVoucherV1 carries nullifier_key and must never travel over this anonymous public GET
body is not an IPPMessage; a landing page served on the JSON leg must not be parsed as one

expect.note: All four skippable bytes (0x0D 0x0A 0x09 0x20) ahead of 0x7B. POSITIVE control for the byte rule: these four and only these four may be skipped.

expect.reason: body begins EF BB BF. Given as BYTES on purpose: this case is worthless as a decoded string, because the decoders disagree about whether the BOM survives. MEASURED on this exact input — Buffer.toString('utf8') and Go string(b) keep U+FEFF, while TextDecoder and Response.text() strip it, so a code-point implementation on the fetch route never sees it and PAYS while the Go route REFUSES

body begins C2 85, the UTF-8 encoding of U+0085 NEL. Not a skippable byte. MEASURED at the implementation layer: one side's whitespace trimmer removed it and accepted, the other did not and refused — the mirror of the BOM case

body begins 0x0B (VT). NOT one of the four skippable bytes. MEASURED: both implementations accepted a VT prefix because neither restricted itself to the four-byte set; U+000C, U+00A0, U+2028 and U+3000 behaved the same way. On bytes every one of them is rejected

the top-level key 'v' is spelled with a backslash escape. MEASURED as a pay/refuse divergence on this exact body: parse first and the key set is {v,network,type,payload} — a subset of the five, so ACCEPT and pay; compare the raw key tokens and the key is the six characters backslash-u-0-0-7-6, not one of the five, so REJECT. A top-level key's literal spelling MUST be one of the five tokens with no escapes, which removes the unescaping step and puts this rule and the duplicate rule both on the bytes

'v' appears twice at the top level. The 'subset of five keys' check runs AFTER a parser folds duplicates, and the folding is parser-defined (last-one-wins, or an error) — so a lenient parser still sees five keys and accepts while a strict one errors and rejects. Forbidding duplicates outright is decidable on the bytes

the compact 'ipp1:' carrier is not a valid link representation. The decoder shared with the Compact carrier WOULD accept this string — the point is that the link body contract does not, and MUST NOT sniff the encoding
'link_expires_in' is a sixth top-level key. The envelope key set is closed and the extension point is `meta`; see envelope.forward_compatibility_commitment

body_json.message: this payment request is no longer active

expect.note: Only reachable on the HTML leg; a wallet that ever sees it MUST still surface the code rather than crash.
Machine codes are an open string (6.2). An unknown code MUST propagate, never crash the wallet.

The NESTED shape, carrying `type`. Mirror of resolve-error-not-found, which is the same failure in the FLAT shape. Both MUST surface the same code; drop either shape and the other's cases still all pass, which is how the nested-only reading survived unnoticed in both SDKs.
Nested with no `type`, so the subclass has to come from the HTTP status. A reader that requires `type` before it will look at `code` drops the code here.

body_json.message: this payment request is no longer active

expect.note: The RETIRED shape: `error` is a STRING and there is no `code`. This is the boundary of the flat reading -- accepting any JSON object carrying a `message` would type this one and hand the caller an error whose machine code is the empty string, which reads as 'the server sent no code' when in fact the body was not the contract. Still refused, still carries the HTTP status, surfaces no code.

`{}` is well-formed JSON and carries none of the envelope fields in either shape. MUST NOT become a typed error with empty fields: an empty `code` is indistinguishable from a code the SDK failed to read.

The open-string property, in the NESTED shape. Widening the ACCEPTED SHAPES must not widen anything about the code itself: an unrecognised code is still surfaced verbatim, never mapped onto a known one and never turned into a rejection. Paired with resolve-error-unknown-code, which is the same code in the flat shape.
